'''II.''' ''n.'' A word having only one signification or meaning; a generic word, or a word predicable of many different species, as ''fish'', ''tree''. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''univocally''' (ū-niv′ọ̄-kal-i), ''adv.'' In a univocal manner; in one sense or tenor; not equivocally; unmistakably.
{{smaller block|The same word may be employed either ''univocally'', equivocally, or analogously.
{{right|''Whately.''}}}}

'''univocation''' (ū-niv-ọ̄-kā′shọn), ''n.'' [= F. ''univocation'' = Sp. ''univocacion'' = Pg. ''univocação'' = It. ''univocazione''; < LL. ''univocus'', having but one meaning: see ''univocal''.] Agreement of name and meaning. ''Whiston.''—'''Limited univocation†''', {{smaller|univocation of a genus, species, difference, property, or accident: opposed to ''transcendent univocation'', such univocation as is possessed by ens, good, true, relation, absolute, etc.}}

'''unjaundiced''' (un-jän′dist), ''a.'' Not jaundiced; hence, not affected by envy, jealousy, etc.
{{smaller block|An ''unjaundiced'' eye.
{{right|''Cowper'', To Dr. Darwin.}}}}

'''unjealous''' (un-jel′us), ''a.'' Not jealous; not suspicious or mistrustful. ''Clarendon.''

'''unjoin''' (un-join′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''unjoynen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''join''.] To separate; disjoin.
{{smaller block|Tigris and Eufrates ''unjoynen'' and departen hir watres.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. meter 1.}}}}

'''unjoint''' (un-joint′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''joint''.] To disjoint; take apart the joints of: as, to ''unjoint'' a fishing-rod.

'''3.''' Not observed; not obeyed, as a command. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iv. § 14.

'''unkind''' (un-kīnd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unkinde'', ''unkynde'', ''uncunde'', ''unkuynde'', ''onkynde'', ''onkende'', < AS. ''uncynde'', ''ungecynde'', not natural, < ''un-'', not, + ''gecynde'', natural, kind: see ''kind''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Not natural; unnatural.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therfor he, of ful avysement,
Nolde never wryte in none of his sermouns
Of swiche ''unkynde'' abhominaciouns.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Man of Law’s Tale, l. 88.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sympathetic; lacking in or not springing from or exhibiting kindness, benevolence, or affection; not kind; harsh; cruel.
{{smaller block|Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove ''unkind.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1. 101.}}}}

'''unkindliness''' (un-kīnd′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unkindly; unkindness; unfavorableness. ''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.

'''unkindly''' (un-kīnd′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unkindely'', ''unkyndely'', ''unkundeliche'', < AS. ''ungecyndelīc'', ''ungecyndlīc'', unnatural, < ''un-'', not, + ''gecyndelīc'', natural, kindly: see ''kindly'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' Unnatural; contrary to nature.
{{smaller block|And gan abhor her brood’s ''unkindly'' crime.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. x. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' Unfavorable; malignant.
{{smaller block|Forbidding every bleak ''unkindly'' fog.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 269.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''3.''' Not kindly; unkind; ungracious: as, an ''unkindly'' manner.

'''unkindly''' (un-kīnd′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unkindely, unkyndely, unkuyndeliche, unkyndelike,'' < AS. *''ungecyndelīce,'' unnaturally, < ''un-,'' not, + ''gecyndelīce,'' naturally: see ''kindly, adv.''] '''1†.''' In a manner contrary to nature; unnaturally.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dronken Loth ''unkyndely''
Lay by his doughtres two unwityngly.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Pardoner’s Tale, l. 23.}}}}
'''2.''' In an unkind manner; without kindness or affection; ungraciously.
{{smaller block|<poem>Something ''unkindly'' she does take it, sir,
To have her husband chosen to her hands.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.,'' King and No King, iii. 1.}}}}

'''unkindness''' (un-kīnd′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unkyndnes;'' < ''unkind'' + ''-ness.''] '''1.''' The state or character of being unkind; want of kindness; want of natural affection; want of good will; ill will.
{{smaller block|Take hede, I praie thee, that our loue be not inuenimed with ''vnkyndnes.'' {{right|''Golden Book,'' ix.}}
Ingratitude, commenly called ''unkyndnesse.''
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot,'' The Governour, ii. 13.}}}}
'''2.''' An unkind act; harsh treatment; an ill turn.
{{smaller block|In all those ''unkindnesses,'' rudenesses, &c., whereof you accuse yourself, I am enforced to acknowledge myself most justly condemned.
{{right|''J. Bradford,'' Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 4.}}}}

'''unkindred†''' (un-kin′dred), ''a.'' Not of the same kindred, blood, race, or kind; not related.
{{smaller block|One . . . of blood ''unkindred'' to your royal house.
{{right|''Rowe,'' Lady Jane Grey, iii.}}}}

'''unkindredly†''' (un-kin′dred-li), ''a.'' Unlike kindred. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|''Unjointing'' the bones. {{right|''Fuller'', Holy War, p. 247.}}}}

'''unjointed''' (un-join′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no joints, nodes, or articulations; inarticulate.—'''2.''' Unjoined; disjointed; disconnected.
{{smaller block|This bald ''unjointed'' chat. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 3. 65.}}}}
'''3.''' Unhinged; out of joint; disarticulated; luxated or dislocated, as a joint.

'''unjoyful''' (un-joi′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unjoyful'', < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''joyful''.] Joyless; unpleasant.
{{smaller block|Thilke thinges . . . shollen ben ''unjoyful'' to thee. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|This ''unjoyful'' set of people. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 16.}}}}

'''unjoyous''' (un-joi′us), ''a.'' Not joyous; not gay or cheerful.
{{smaller block|Where nothing can be hearty, it must be ''unjoyous'' and injurious to any perceiving person. {{right|''Milton'', Tetrachordon.}}}}

'''unjoyously''' (un-joi′us-li), ''adv.'' In an unjoyous manner; joylessly.

'''unjust''' (un-just′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unjust''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''just''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Not just. {{smaller|(''a'') Not acting or disposed to act according to law and justice; not upright.}}
{{smaller block|He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the ''unjust''. {{right|Mat. v. 45.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Contrary to justice and right; wrongful; unjustifiable.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This is a signe, for-sothe, of a sure, Emperour,
And the coniunctoun ''vniust'' is Joynit vs betwene,
Is care for to come, with a cold ende.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 13831.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And my more-having would be as a sauce
To make me hunger more; that I should forge
Quarrels ''unjust'' against the good and loyal.</poem> {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 83.}}}}
'''2†.''' Dishonest; faithless; perfidious.
{{smaller block|Gentlemen of companies, . . . and such as indeed were never soldiers, but discarded ''unjust'' serving-men.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 2. 30.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' Inequitable, unfair, unrighteous. See ''righteous.''

'''unjustice''' (un-jus′tis), ''n.'' Injustice. ''Hales'', Sermon, Rom. xiv. 1.

'''unjustifiable''' (un-jus′ti-fī-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not justifiable; not defensible or right.
{{smaller block|The foolish and ''unjustifiable'' doctrine of indulgences.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Of Repentance, ii. 1.}}}}

'''unjustifiableness''' (un-jus′ti-fī-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unjustifiable. ''Clarendon.''

'''unjustifiably''' (un-jus′ti-fī-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a manner that cannot be justified or vindicated. ''Burke'', Rev. in France.

'''unjustly''' (un-just′li), ''adv.'' In an unjust manner; wrongfully. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 40.

'''unjustness''' (un-just′nes), ''n.'' The character of being unjust; injustice.

'''unked''' (ung′ked), ''a.'' [Also ''unkid'', ''unketh'', ''unkith'', ''unkard;'' dial. vars. of ''uncouth:'' see ''uncouth'', and cf. ''unco.''] Unusual; odd; strange; ugly; hence, solitary; dangerous. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|It seemed an ''unked'' place for an unarmed man to venture through. {{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, xxxi.}}}}

'''unkembed†''', '''unkemmed†''' (un-kemd′), ''a.'' Same as ''unkempt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Her head
With long ''unkemb’d'' haire loaden.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Sophonisba, iv. 1.}}
With long ''unkemmed'' hairs. {{right|''May'', tr. of Lucan’s Pharsalia, vi.}}}}

'''unkempt''' (un-kemt′), ''a.'' [A later form of ''unkembed'', also ''unkemmed''; < ME. ''unkempt''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''kembed'', ''kempt'', pp. of ''kemb''.] '''1.''' Uncombed; disheveled: as, ''unkempt'' hair; hence, disorderly. —'''2.''' Figuratively, rough; unpolished.
{{smaller block|<poem>But ah! too well I wote my humble vaine,
And howe my rimes bene rugged and ''unkempt''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., November.}}
The aspect of some lawless, ''unkempt'' genius.
{{right|''M. C. Tyler'', Life of Patrick Henry, p. 16.}}}}

'''unkenned''' (un-kend′), ''a.'' [Also ''unkend'', ''unkent''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''kenned'', pp. of ''ken''<sup>1</sup>.] Unknown. [Obsolete or dialectal.]
{{smaller block|To travel through ''unkenned'' lands.
{{right|''Greene'', Alphonsus, iv.}}}}

'''unkennel''' (un-ken′el), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unkenneled'', ''unkennelled'', ppr. ''unkenneling'', ''unkennelling''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''kennel''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To drive or force from a kennel; take out of a kennel. ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3. 174.—'''2.''' To rouse from secrecy or retreat.
{{smaller block|<poem>Observe mine uncle, if his occulted guilt
Do not itself ''unkennel'' in one speech.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 86.}}}}

'''unkensome†''' (un-ken′sum), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ken''<sup>1</sup> + ''-some''.] Not recognizable.
{{smaller block|It ’s ''unkensome'' we wad be.
{{right|''Archie of Ca’field'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 90).}}}}

'''unkept''' (un-kept′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not kept; not retained; not preserved.—'''2.''' Not sustained, maintained, or tended.
{{smaller block|He . . . stays me here at home ''unkept''.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 1. 9.}}}} '''3.''' Not observed; not obeyed, as a command. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iv. § 14.

'''unkind''' (un-kīnd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unkinde'', ''unkynde'', ''uncunde'', ''unkuynde'', ''onkynde'', ''onkende'', < AS. ''uncynde'', ''ungecynde'', not natural, < ''un-'', not, + ''gecynde'', natural, kind: see ''kind''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Not natural; unnatural.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therfor he, of ful avysement,
Nolde never wryte in none of his sermouns
Of swiche ''unkynde'' abhominaciouns.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Man of Law’s Tale, l. 88.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sympathetic; lacking in or not springing from or exhibiting kindness, benevolence, or affection; not kind; harsh; cruel.
{{smaller block|Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove ''unkind.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1. 101.}}}}

'''unkindliness''' (un-kīnd′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unkindly; unkindness; unfavorableness. ''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.

'''unkindly''' (un-kīnd′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unkindely'', ''unkyndely'', ''unkundeliche'', < AS. ''ungecyndelīc'', ''ungecyndlīc'', unnatural, < ''un-'', not, + ''gecyndelīc'', natural, kindly: see ''kindly'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' Unnatural; contrary to nature.
{{smaller block|And gan abhor her brood’s ''unkindly'' crime.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. x. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' Unfavorable; malignant.
{{smaller block|Forbidding every bleak ''unkindly'' fog.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 269.}}}}

'''3.''' Not kindly; unkind; ungracious: as, an ''unkindly'' manner.

'''unkindly''' (un-kīnd′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unkindely, unkyndely, unkuyndeliche, unkyndelike,'' < AS. *''ungecyndelīce,'' unnaturally, < ''un-,'' not, + ''gecyndelīce,'' naturally: see ''kindly, adv.''] '''1†.''' In a manner contrary to nature; unnaturally.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dronken Loth ''unkyndely''
Lay by his doughtres two unwityngly.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Pardoner’s Tale, l. 23.}}}}
'''2.''' In an unkind manner; without kindness or affection; ungraciously.
{{smaller block|<poem>Something ''unkindly'' she does take it, sir,
To have her husband chosen to her hands.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.,'' King and No King, iii. 1.}}}}

'''unkindness''' (un-kīnd′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unkyndnes;'' < ''unkind'' + ''-ness.''] '''1.''' The state or character of being unkind; want of kindness; want of natural affection; want of good will; ill will.
{{smaller block|Take hede, I praie thee, that our loue be not inuenimed with ''vnkyndnes.'' {{right|''Golden Book,'' ix.}}
Ingratitude, commenly called ''unkyndnesse.''
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot,'' The Governour, ii. 13.}}}}
'''2.''' An unkind act; harsh treatment; an ill turn.
{{smaller block|In all those ''unkindnesses,'' rudenesses, &c., whereof you accuse yourself, I am enforced to acknowledge myself most justly condemned.
{{right|''J. Bradford,'' Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 4.}}}}

'''unkindred†''' (un-kin′dred), ''a.'' Not of the same kindred, blood, race, or kind; not related.
{{smaller block|One . . . of blood ''unkindred'' to your royal house.
{{right|''Rowe,'' Lady Jane Grey, iii.}}}}

'''unkindredly†''' (un-kin′dred-li), ''a.'' Unlike kindred. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Her ''unkindredly'' kin.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 391. (''Davies.'')}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
